elements.id-string-3: Reinforcement Learning (RL) has been successful in various domains like robotics, game playing, and simulation.While RL agents have shown impressive capabilities in their specific tasks, they insufficiently adapt to new tasks.In supervised learning, this adaptation problem is addressed by large-scale pre-training followed by fine-tuning to new down-stream tasks.Recently, pre-training on multiple tasks has been gaining traction in RL.However, fine-tuning a pre-trained model often suffers from catastrophic forgetting, that is, the performance on the pre-training tasks deteriorates when fine-tuning on new tasks.To investigate the catastrophic forgetting phenomenon, we first jointly pre-train a model on datasets from two benchmark suites, namely Meta-World and DMControl.Then, we evaluate and compare a variety of fine-tuning methods prevalent in natural language processing, both in terms of performance on new tasks, and how well performance on pre-training tasks is retained.Our study shows that with most fine-tuning approaches, the performance on pre-training tasks deteriorates significantly.Therefore, we propose a novel method, Learning-to-Modulate (L2M), that avoids the degradation of learned skills by modulating the information flow of the frozen pre-trained model via a learnable modulation pool.Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Continual-World benchmark, while retaining performance on the pre-training tasks.Finally, to aid future research in this area, we release a dataset encompassing $50$ Meta-World and $16$ DMControl tasks.
elements.id-string-5: Reinforcement Learning (RL) has been instrumental in training agents capable of achieving notable successes, both in simulation, and in the real-world \citep{Silver:16, Vinyals:19,Berner:19,Arjona:19,Bellemare:20,Degrave:2022}.
elements.id-string-6: However, such agents are usually highly specialized and incapable of performing well outside of a narrowly-defined task.
elements.id-string-7: Furthermore, adapting a pre-trained agent to a new task by fine-tuning usually results in decreased performance on prior tasks.
elements.id-string-8: This effect is well-known in the literature as \textit{catastrophic forgetting} \citep{McCloskey:1989}.
elements.id-string-9: A common paradigm to learn multiple tasks concurrently is multi-task learning \citep{caruana:97}.
elements.id-string-10: However, typically, not all tasks we want an agent to learn are available at training time.
elements.id-string-11: In this case, new tasks must be learned in a sequential manner.
elements.id-string-12: Learning a new task ideally exploits knowledge from previously learned tasks and does not adversely affect the performance on these prior tasks.
elements.id-string-13: Recent works have demonstrated that models based on the Transformer architecture \citep{Vaswani:17} excel at learning multiple tasks concurrently from large offline datasets \citep{Lee:22,Reed:22,Jiang:22,Brohan:22,Gupta:22,Shridar:22}.
elements.id-string-14: We want to utilize this capability in RL, thereby obtaining agents that can quickly learn new skills and adapt to new tasks.
elements.id-string-15: However, it is still unclear how an agent can learn new tasks and skills without negatively impacting its performance on the tasks it has already learned.

elements.id-string-17: Our aim is to find methods that enable an agent to efficiently learn new tasks without compromising its proficiency in previously acquired tasks.
elements.id-string-18: In this regard, we draw inspiration from fine-tuning (FT) techniques prevalent in supervised learning, such as parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT,~\citep{Houlsby:19,Hu:21,Liu:22}) and prompt-based tuning (PBT,~\citep{Lester:21,Xiang:21}).
elements.id-string-19: Both PBT, and PEFT, incorporate a small set of new parameters to adapt a pre-trained model to new tasks at low cost.
elements.id-string-20: Thus, they intrinsically avoid catastrophic forgetting.
elements.id-string-21: However, it is unclear how well these methods can be adopted for training RL agents from offline datasets.
elements.id-string-22: Therefore, we first conduct a comprehensive evaluation for fine-tuning a pretrained Decision Transformer (DT, \citealp{Chen:21})
elements.id-string-23: on two established RL benchmarks, namely Meta-World~\citep{Yu:22,Wolczyk:21} and DMControl~\citep{Tassa:18}.
elements.id-string-24: We first pre-train a DT jointly on tasks from both domains, before adapting the pre-trained model to new tasks using various FT, PEFT and PBT methods (Figure \ref{fig:mddt}).
elements.id-string-25: We find that FT methods adjust well to new tasks, but performance on previous tasks generally decreases.
elements.id-string-26: PBT, in contrast, retains performance on previous tasks but does not adapt well to new tasks.

elements.id-string-33: L2M operates in a task-agnostic manner and efficiently adapts a pre-trained model to new tasks via a learnable modulation pool.
elements.id-string-34: The modulation pool consists of learnable keys that are associated with learnable modulation matrices.
elements.id-string-35: Based on the current context, L2M selects a set of modulators which are learned during fine-tuning on the new task.

elements.id-string-46: \textbf{Reinforcement Learning.} We consider a Markov decision process (MDP) represented by the tuple  $(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{P},\mathcal{R})$.
elements.id-string-47: $\mathcal{S}$ and $\mathcal{A}$ denote state and action spaces, respectively, with states $s_t \in \mathcal{S}$ and actions $a_t \in \mathcal{A}$ at timestep $t$.
elements.id-string-48: The transition function $\mathcal{P}(s_{t+1}\mid s_t, a_t)$ takes a state-action pair and yields a probability distribution over next states.
elements.id-string-49: The reward function $\mathcal{R}(r_t \mid s_t, a_t)$ maps a given state-action pair to a scalar reward $r_t$.
elements.id-string-50: The objective is to learn a policy $\pi(a_t\mid s_t)$ that predicts an action $a_t$ given $s_t$ that maximizes the reward $r_t$.
elements.id-string-51: \textbf{Decision Transformer.} Decision Transformer (DT, \citealp{Chen:21}) rephrases RL as a sequence modelling problem.
elements.id-string-52: This assumes access to a dataset $\mathcal{D}=\{\tau_i \mid 1 \leq i \leq B \}$, where $\tau_i=(s_0, a_0, r_0, \ldots, s_T, a_T, r_T)$ represents a trajectory consisting of state-action-reward triplets and $B$ defines the number of trajectories in $\mathcal{D}$.
elements.id-string-53: Further, they follow the definition of upside-down-RL \citep{Schmidhuber:19} and augment each trajectory $\tau_i$ with \emph{returns-to-go} $\hat R_t=\sum_{t'=t}^T r_{t'}$.
elements.id-string-54: The policy $\pi_{\theta} (a_t \mid s_{t-K: t}, \hat R_{t-K:t}, a_{t-K:t-1}, r_{t-K:t-1})$, with parameters $\theta$ and context length $K$, is then trained in a supervised manner.
elements.id-string-55: During inference, the policy produces a sequence of actions conditioned on a high return-to-go.

elements.id-string-66: We propose L2M, a method that combines the advantages of parameter-efficient fine-tuning and prompt-based tuning approaches.
elements.id-string-67: In particular, we rely on PEFT methods, such as LoRA (\citealp{Hu:21}), which we refer to as modulators of the pre-trained model.
elements.id-string-68: Similar to Learning-to-prompt (L2P, \citealp{Wang:22}), we maintain a pool of modulators associated with learnable keys.
elements.id-string-69: For a given input sequence, we retrieve the best modulator weights from the pool, and leverage them to alter the behaviour of the pretrained model (Figure \ref{fig:l2m-architecture}).
elements.id-string-70: We define a \emph{modulation pool} that contains a set of $M$ keys, $\mathbf{K}_{\text{pool}} = \{\mathbf{k}_i \mid 1 \leq i \leq M \}$.
elements.id-string-71: Each $\mathbf{k}_i$ is associated with a set of modulation matrices $\{ \mathbf{A}_{b}^i, \mathbf{B}_{b}^i \}$, for each layer block $b$ of a DT with $B$ layer blocks.
elements.id-string-72: At time $t$, we compose all states in a trajectory $\tau$ into a matrix $\mathbf{S}_{\leq t}$ after they are processed via the embedding layer of the DT.
elements.id-string-73: Subsequently, we reduce the matrix to a query vector $\mathbf{q}_t \in \mathbb{R}^{d_q}$ by an aggregation function $g(\cdot)$:
elements.id-string-75: For the aggregation function $g(\cdot)$, we use mean-pooling.
elements.id-string-76: Further, we retrieve a set of modulation matrices $\{ \mathbf{A}_{b}^j, \mathbf{B}_{b}^j \mid 1 \leq b \leq B\}$ by the maximum similarity between each $\mathbf{k} \in \mathbf{K}_{\text{pool}}$ and the query $\mathbf{q}_t$ at timestep $t$:
elements.id-string-78: In our case, $\text{sim}(\cdot, \cdot)$ corresponds to the cosine similarity and $n(\mathbf{k})^{-1}$ represents the inverse selection count for key $\mathbf{k}$ up to the current task.
elements.id-string-79: This way, we discourage that queries for different tasks attend to the same key.
elements.id-string-80: We use $\{ \mathbf{A}_{b}^j, \mathbf{B}_{b}^j \mid 1 \leq b \leq B\}$ to modulate the DT according to \cref{eq:lora}.
elements.id-string-81: More specifically, we employ LoRA on the queries and values in the attention mechanism, as well as on the activation in the feed-forward block in the pre-trained DT.
elements.id-string-82: Subsequently, we learn the weights of the module using gradient descent while keeping the pretrained model frozen.
elements.id-string-83: Following \citet{Wang:22}, the key is updated by maximizing the cosine similarity between $\mathbf{q}_t$ and $\mathbf{k}_j$ via an additional term in the end-to-end loss function.
elements.id-string-84: Similar to \citet{Hu:21}, we initialize $\mathbf{A}$ according to a normal distribution around zero and $\mathbf{B}$ with zeros.

elements.id-string-86: All keys in $\mathbf{K}_{\text{pool}}$ are initialized uniformly from $[-1, 1]$.

elements.id-string-224: \textbf{Transformers in RL.} Since the inception of Transformers \citep{Vaswani:17} there has been a widespread adoption of the underlying architecture in many areas of Machine Learning research such as NLP \citep{Devlin:18,Radford:19,Brown:20}, computer vision \citep{Dosovitskiy:21,He:22,Radford:21,Fürst:21,Ramesh:21,Rombach:22}, speech recognition \citep{Radford:22,Baevski:20} or video generation \citep{Ho:22,Singer:22}.
elements.id-string-225: More recently, Transformers have found their way into RL.
elements.id-string-226: Similar to the DT \citet{Chen:21}, Trajectory Transformer \citep{Janner:21} is based on the GPT architecture \citep{Radford:18}, but relies on dynamics modelling.
elements.id-string-227: \citet{Lee:22} extended DT to a multi-game setup to learn to play 46 Atari games.
elements.id-string-228: Meanwhile, a variety of DT-variants have been proposed \citep{Zheng:22,Wang_bootstrapped:22,Shang:22,Meng:21}.
elements.id-string-229: \citet{Siebenborn:22} replace the Transformer in DT with an LSTM \citep{Hochreiter:97}.
elements.id-string-230: PromptDT \citep{Xu:22} demonstrated that prompting a pre-trained DT model with expert trajectories can improve the agent's ability to generalize to new tasks.
elements.id-string-231: However, the tasks they consider do not differ substantially.
elements.id-string-232: \citet{Jiang:22} presented a prompt-based Transformer for robot manipulation, that integrates multi-modal prompts via cross-attention.
elements.id-string-233: \citet{Reed:22} trained a Transformer that scaled to over 600 tasks.
elements.id-string-234: Most recently, \citet{Brohan:22} presented a scalable Transformer for real-world robotics manipulation.
elements.id-string-235: \citet{Laskin:22} and \citet{Liu:23} make use of a multi-episodic context to elicit in-context learning capabilities.
elements.id-string-236: Other works use a Transformer backbone for history compression in online RL \citep{Parisotto:20,Paischer:22,Paischer:23}.
elements.id-string-237: \citet{Li:23} and \citet{Yang:23} cover the landscape of Transformers in RL in more detail.
elements.id-string-239: A plethora of works have considered learning multiple tasks concurrently via RL \citep{Tanaka:03,Rusu:policy:16,Borsa:16,Rajeswaran:17,Bsat:17,Andreas:17,Deramo:20,Yu:20,Igl:20,Sodhani:21}.
elements.id-string-240: In CRL, however, tasks are considered to not be readily available at the same time.
elements.id-string-241: Many CRL methods were proposed for computer vision, but can also be applied to a CRL setting.
elements.id-string-242: Early works include regularization approaches, such as EWC \citep{Kirkpatrick:17}, Synaptic Intelligence \citep{Zenke:17}, Memory-aware Synapses \citep{Aljundi:18}, Gradient Episodic Memory (GEM, \citealp{Lopez:17}) and A-GEM \citep{Chaudhry:18}.
elements.id-string-243: Other approaches rely on adding new modules to existing architecture \citep{Rusu:16}, iterative pruning \citep{Mallya:18}, or improved exploration \citep{Steinparz:22}.
elements.id-string-244: A number of approaches have been tested on the Continual-World benchmark \citep{Wolczyk:21}, including 3RL \citep{Caccia:22}, ClonExSAC \citep{Wolczyk:22} and Modulating masks \citep{Ben:22}.
elements.id-string-245: L2P \citep{Wang:22} learns to prompt a frozen Vision Transformer \citep{Dosovitskiy:21} and consistently outperforms prior methods on a number of CL benchmarks.
elements.id-string-246: Other follow-up works that rely on a prompting mechanism for CL have been proposed \citep{Wang_dual:22, Smith:22, Razdaibiedina:23}.
elements.id-string-247: Recent works provide a comprehensive overview of the field of CRL \citep{Hadsell:20,Lesort:20,Khetarpal:22,Baker:23}.
elements.id-string-248: \textbf{Parameter-efficient fine-tuning and Prompting.} Large-language models (LLMs) are usually pre-trained on vast amounts of data \cite{Devlin:18,Radford:19,Brown:20}.
elements.id-string-249: After pre-training, it is desirable to specialize or fine-tune the foundation model \citep{Bommasani:21} to a down-stream task.
elements.id-string-250: A common way is fine-tuning all network weights or a fraction thereof.
elements.id-string-251: Fine-tuning the entire network is costly and suffers from catastrophic forgetting.
elements.id-string-252: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods and prompt-based tuning offer attractive alternatives.
elements.id-string-253: \citet{Houlsby:19} repurposed Adapter modules \citep{Rebuffi:17} to interleave pretrained Transformer layers.
elements.id-string-255: Low Rank Adaptation injects trainable low-rank decomposition matrices into every layer of the model \citep{Hu:21}.
elements.id-string-256: (IA$\text{)}^3$ modulates the inner activation flow of the Transformer layers by elementwise multiplication with learned modulation vectors \citep{Liu:22}.
elements.id-string-257: Prompt tuning conditions the pre-trained model on new tasks by prepending learnable prompts to the embedded input sequence \citep{Lester:21}.
elements.id-string-258: Similarly, prefix-tuning adds learnable prefix vectors to the keys and values of each attention head input \cite{Xiang:21}.
elements.id-string-259: P-tuning v2, applies learnable prompts at each Transformer layer, instead of merely the input layer \citep{Liu:21a}.

elements.id-string-263: Adapting agents to new tasks, while preserving performance on previously learned tasks, remains a major challenge towards more general RL agents.
elements.id-string-264: Consequently, we conduct a comprehensive evaluation of established fine-tuning, PEFT and PBT methods for Transformers in RL.
elements.id-string-265: We evaluate both how well new tasks are learned and how strongly performance deteriorates on the pre-training tasks.
elements.id-string-266: While full fine-tuning of a pre-trained model adapts well to new tasks, it suffers from catastrophic forgetting of pre-training tasks.
elements.id-string-267: Prompt-based tuning techniques preserve performance on pre-training tasks, but cannot compete on new tasks.
elements.id-string-268: We propose a novel method, L2M, which performs well in both dimensions.
elements.id-string-269: L2M enables efficient fine-tuning of pre-trained models via learnable modulation matrices, resulting in high performance both on new tasks and on pre-training tasks.
elements.id-string-270: Finally, we release a large dataset of trajectories for the Meta-World and DMControl benchmark suites to facilitate future research in the domain of offline RL.
elements.id-string-271: For future work, we envision an investigation on the compositionality of learned modulation matrices.
elements.id-string-272: While currently a distinct set of modulators is selected for a given input sequence, we believe that by combining and sharing modulators across tasks, our method can improve in terms of performance as well as in parameter-efficiency.
elements.id-string-273: Such an approach could improve forward-transfer, where new tasks benefit even more from previously learned tasks by combining existing skills.
elements.id-string-274: Furthermore, the context length of the models we consider is currently limited.
elements.id-string-275: Extending the context to leverage information from multiple episodes and tasks may improve the model's ability to generalize to new tasks or domains.
elements.id-string-276: Another promising avenue of research is to investigate more diverse domains and explore how different fine-tuning methods perform on more distinct fine-tuning domains.

elements.id-string-288: For our experiments, we use environments from the Meta-World benchmark \citep{Yu:22}.
elements.id-string-289: Meta-World tasks consist of a Sawyer robotic arm simulated using the MuJoCo physics engine \citep{Todorov:12}.
elements.id-string-290: The observation space in Meta-World is a 39-dimensional vector.
elements.id-string-291: The action space is 4-dimensional, with all actions in range $[-1, 1]$.
elements.id-string-292: For each environment, the reward functions are scaled to have a maximum value of 10 and a minimum of 0.
elements.id-string-293: The exact reward-function definitions are provided in \citet{Yu:22}.
elements.id-string-294: Episodes are 200 timesteps long in all environments.
elements.id-string-295: For all our experiments on Meta-World environments, we report success rates and mean rewards obtained.
elements.id-string-296: \textbf{Difference between Meta-World v1 and v2 environments.} The Continual-World benchmark was published using v1 of Meta-World.
elements.id-string-297: However, in the meantime v2 has been released.
elements.id-string-298: While the v1 environments had a 9 dimensional observation space, the observation space is 39-diemsional in v2.
elements.id-string-299: Another major change in v2, was the introduction of dense and bounded reward functions.
elements.id-string-301: The Continual-World benchmark was proposed by \citet{Wolczyk:21} and is built on top of Meta-World.
elements.id-string-302: Continual-World is a challenging CRL benchmark, consisting of 10 of the 50 tasks contained in Meta-World, denoted as CW10.
elements.id-string-303: We use the tasks contained in CW10 as fine-tuning set and select the remaining 40 tasks as pre-training set (MT40).
elements.id-string-308: The DMControl Suite benchmark \citep{Tassa:18} consists of 30 simulated continuous control tasks built on the MuJoCo physics engine.
elements.id-string-309: DMControl encompasses a wide variety of robot morphologies, ranging from a simple cartpole to a complex humanoid.
elements.id-string-310: Therefore, the observation and action spaces vary across environments.
elements.id-string-311: The action spaces vary between 1 (\texttt{cartpole}) and 21 continuous dimensions (\texttt{humanoid}), where each action dimension is bounded by $[-1, 1]$.
elements.id-string-312: Agents can be trained based on continuous vector-based representations (state-based) or directly from pixels (pixel-based).
elements.id-string-313: In this work, we focus on the state-based representations, which vary between 3 (\texttt{pendulum}) and 67 continuous dimensions (\texttt{humanoid}).
elements.id-string-314: As described in Section \ref{sec:experiments}, we select 16 of the 30 DMControl tasks and assign 10 to the pre-training set (DMC10) and 6 to the fine-tuning set (DMC6).

elements.id-string-325: \textbf{Fine-tuning.} In full fine-tuning, the entire pre-trained model is trained on the new task.
elements.id-string-326: We also try other common variations thereof, such as fine-tuning the action head, the last layer, or both.
elements.id-string-327: \textbf{Adapters.} Adapters are a parameter-efficient fine-tuning approach proposed by \citet{Houlsby:19}.
elements.id-string-328: An adapter layer consists of a down-projection, a non-linearity and an up-projection along with a skip connection.
elements.id-string-329: Two Adapter modules are added to every Transformer block.
elements.id-string-330: During training, only the Adapters (and optionally LayerNorms) are updated, while the remaining parameters are kept frozen.
elements.id-string-331: This significantly reduces the number of trainable parameters, while preserving the ability to adapt to new tasks.
elements.id-string-332: \citet{Houlsby:19} adapt a BERT \citep{Devlin:18}  model to 26 different text classification tasks, while training only roughly 4\% of the parameters and attaining performance close to full fine-tuning.
elements.id-string-333: \textbf{LoRA.} LoRA was proposed by \citep{Hu:21} and is discussed in more detail in Section \ref{sec:method}.
elements.id-string-334: \textbf{(IA$\text{)}^3$: Infused Adapter by Inhibiting and Amplifying Inner Activations.}.
elements.id-string-335: Similar to LoRA, (IA$\text{)}^3$ \citep{Liu:22} modulates the inner activation flow of the Transformer layers and can be applied to every component of the pre-trained model.
elements.id-string-336: Instead of low-rank modulation matrices as used in LoRA, (IA$\text{)}^3$ performs elementwise multiplication with learnable modulation vectors.
elements.id-string-337: Thus, (IA$\text{)}^3$ typically incurs less additional parameters compared to other methods.
elements.id-string-338: \textbf{Prompt-tuning.} \citet{Lester:21} learn soft prompts to enable a frozen pre-trained GPT-3 \citep{Brown:20} model to generalize to downstream tasks.
elements.id-string-339: In prompt-tuning, the learnable prompts are prepended to the input sequence, while the rest of the pre-trained model is kept frozen.
elements.id-string-340: This allows to effectively separate the learnable task parameters from the model parameters.
elements.id-string-342: Similar to prompt-tuning, prefix-tuning prepends learnable vectors (i.e., soft-prompts) to the input.
elements.id-string-343: However, unlike in prompt-tuning, the learnable prompts are prepended to the keys and values of the attention head input.
elements.id-string-344: Therefore, prefix-tuning also incurs more parameters than prompt-tuning, but typically results in better performance.
elements.id-string-345: \textbf{P-tuning v2.} \citet{Liu:21a} proposed P-tuning v2 as a successor of prefix-tuning.
elements.id-string-346: Instead of prepending continuous prompts only on the input layer, P-tuning v2 prepends them for every layer of the pre-trained model.
elements.id-string-347: This simple modification results in more parameters, but better performance.
elements.id-string-348: In particular, P-tuning v2 matches the performance of full fine-tuning on a number of NLP benchmarks and is effective across model sizes (330M to 10B parameters).
elements.id-string-349: \textbf{EWC and L2.} EWC \citep{Kirkpatrick:17} is an established technique for continual learning based on regularization.
elements.id-string-350: EWC helps to prevent forgetting of previous tasks when learning a new task by protecting parameters that are important for previously learned tasks.
elements.id-string-351: EWC uses the Fisher information matrix as a regularization term, which measures the sensitivity of each parameter with respect to each task and, thus, indicates which parameters require protection.
elements.id-string-352: L2 is used as a baseline in the original EWC publication \citep{Kirkpatrick:17} and utilizes the L2 penalty to protect previously learned weights.
elements.id-string-353: In this section, we describe our Multi-Domain Decision Transformer (MDDT) architecture in more detail (also see Section \ref{sec:method}).
elements.id-string-354: We pre-train a MDDT on the 50 collected pre-training datasets simultaneously (Section \ref{sec:exp-pretrain}).
elements.id-string-355: Then we fine-tune the pre-trained model to 16 new tasks from two domains.
elements.id-string-356: To achieve this, we extend the DT architecture proposed by \citet{Chen:21} to handle inputs from multiple domains with varying state and/or action spaces.
elements.id-string-358: While all Meta-World environments share a 39-dimensional state-space, the dimensionalities of the state-spaces in DMControl vary between 3 and 67 continuous values (See Appendix \ref{appendix:environments}).
elements.id-string-359: This variation reflects the diverse robot morphologies across DMControl tasks.
elements.id-string-360: To deal with these heterogeneous state spaces, we construct a unified state-space that spans all dimension of DMControl and Meta-World environments.
elements.id-string-361: While the dimensionalities of state-spaces differ between environments, they may share common observation types, such as orientation, current velocity, or arm positions of the robot.
elements.id-string-362: In total, DMControl encompasses 24 different observation types.
elements.id-string-363: Our constructed state-space unifies all of these observation-type attributes, amounting to 204 continuous dimensions in total.
elements.id-string-364: For example, the first 13 dimensions correspond to the current orientations of the robot and the last dimension corresponds to the current height.
elements.id-string-365: Dimensions that are unused by a certain environment are zero-padded.
elements.id-string-366: For Meta-World, we pad the 39-dimensional states with zeros to 204 dimensions in total.
elements.id-string-367: Thus, the constructed state-space covers all environments considered in this work.
elements.id-string-368: Finally, as in the original DT publication \citep{Chen:21}, the states are embedded with a linear layer before serving as input to the MDDT.
elements.id-string-369: The full procedure is available in the accompanying source code.
elements.id-string-370: We choose this scheme for handling varying state-spaces instead of discretisation followed by padding, as was used in prior work \citep{Reed:22}.
elements.id-string-371: Discretisation of states in combination with padding drastically increases the context length and, thus, the computational requirements.
elements.id-string-372: For example, when tokenizing a 5 timesteps long trajectory in Meta-World, the context would expand to 195 tokens (39 dimensions * 5 timesteps) for states alone.
elements.id-string-373: In contrast, our scheme results in only 5 state tokens.
elements.id-string-375: To handle action spaces of varying dimensionalities, we tokenise each action dimension and autoregressively predict action tokens, similar to \citet{Reed:22} and \citet{Brohan:22}.
elements.id-string-376: In the environments we consider, the action-spaces vary between 1 and 6 dimensions and all actions are bounded by [-1, 1].
elements.id-string-377: We use a min-max tokenization to discretise every continuous action dimensions into 64 bins and then pad to the maximum action dimension.
elements.id-string-378: Thus, we obtain 6 discrete action tokens from every action.
elements.id-string-379: During evaluation, we autoregressively predict the action tokens until the dimensionality of action space in the particular environment is reached, and then execute the composed action.
elements.id-string-380: Note that autoregressive prediction of actions make the prediction task harder, when compared to predicting all dimensions at once, as is commonly done for
elements.id-string-382: We leave this for future work.
elements.id-string-384: Similar to \citet{Lee:22}, the policy $\pi_{\theta}$ with trainable parameters $\theta$, predicts the next action $a_t$ from a given context of the $K$ most recent states, RTGs, actions and rewards.
elements.id-string-385: States and actions are pre-processed as described earlier, and then embedded using separate linear layers.
elements.id-string-386: Similarly, we embed the continuous scalars for RTGs and rewards using linear layers.
elements.id-string-387: Unlike we \citet{Lee:22}, we do not discretise rewards or RTGs.
elements.id-string-388: However, similar to \citet{Chen:21}, we scale the rewards and RTGs such that all RTGs lie roughly within the range [0, 10].
elements.id-string-389: To achieve this, we use separate reward scales per domain of 200 and 100 for Meta-World and DMControl, respectively.
elements.id-string-390: Thus, each timestep is made up of 9 embedded tokens (1$\times$ state, 1$\times$ RTG, 6 $\times$ action, 1 $\times$ reward).
elements.id-string-391: We use a context-length of 5 timesteps for all our experiments, and therefore, the final sequence length expands to 45 embedded tokens (5 timesteps * 9 tokens per timestep).
elements.id-string-392: \textbf{Positional encodings.} Once the sequence is embedded, we add positional information to every embedded token.
elements.id-string-393: As \citet{Chen:21}, we learn an embedding for each timestep and add this embedding to every embedded token in a timestep.
elements.id-string-394: This approach is different to standard positional embeddings, as every timestep corresponds to 9 tokens.
elements.id-string-395: In addition to the local positional information of how tokens relate to each other within a sequence, this approach also contains global positional information of where a timestep is located within a trajectory.
elements.id-string-396: For example, the choice for an action may differ at the beginning vs.
elements.id-string-397: at the end of an episode.
elements.id-string-398: We also explored other positional encodings in preliminary experiments, but found learned time-step based embeddings to work best.
elements.id-string-400: In line with prior work \citep{Chen:21, Lee:22}, we train the DT via return-conditioned upside-down RL using a cross-entropy loss to predict next actions.
elements.id-string-401: Unlike \citet{Lee:22}, during evaluation we set the target return to the maximum observed return in the respective dataset, instead of utilizing their proposed expert-action inference mechanism.
elements.id-string-402: However, we also found that constant proxies per domain (e.g., 2000  and 1000) work well.

elements.id-string-597: Reinforcement Learning (RL) has been successful in various domains like robotics, game playing, and simulation.While RL agents have shown impressive capabilities in their specific tasks, they insufficiently adapt to new tasks.In supervised learning, this adaptation problem is addressed by large-scale pre-training followed by fine-tuning to new down-stream tasks.Recently, pre-training on multiple tasks has been gaining traction in RL.However, fine-tuning a pre-trained model often suffers from catastrophic forgetting.That is, the performance on the pre-training tasks deteriorates when fine-tuning on new tasks.To investigate the catastrophic forgetting phenomenon, we first jointly pre-train a model on datasets from two benchmark suites, namely Meta-World and DMControl.Then, we evaluate and compare a variety of fine-tuning methods prevalent in natural language processing, both in terms of performance on new tasks, and how well performance on pre-training tasks is retained.Our study shows that with most fine-tuning approaches, the performance on pre-training tasks deteriorates significantly.Therefore, we propose a novel method, Learning-to-Modulate (L2M), that avoids the degradation of learned skills by modulating the information flow of the frozen pre-trained model via a learnable modulation pool.Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Continual-World benchmark, while retaining performance on the pre-training tasks.Finally, to aid future research in this area, we release a dataset encompassing $50$ Meta-World and $16$ DMControl tasks.
